voiceover.text: We've followed the chain of determinants for whole groups. Now let's point it at one group, young people. Think of someone who was sixteen about thirty years ago, a parent, an aunt or a teacher. What was the same about being sixteen then, and what's changed? People love to answer that with a strong opinion. Today, we'll answer it with a method.

Start with what's constant. Adolescence, the stage between childhood and adulthood, comes with the same developmental tasks in every generation we have records for. Your body changes faster than your sense of yourself. Your reasoning grows. You work out who you are, separately from your family, which is called identity formation. Friends start to matter more than family. And you take over decisions that used to be made for you, which is autonomy. One more constant: the brain's reward system tends to mature earlier than its impulse control, so risk-taking rises in every generation.

scenes.title: what the constants mean for health

voiceover.text: These constants matter for health. More risk-taking is why injury is a leading cause of harm for young people, generation after generation. Friends mattering more is why programs run by peers often work better than lectures from adults. And growing autonomy is why habits set in adolescence tend to last. But don't turn this into a deficit story. The same brain that takes more risks also learns fast, adapts quickly and tries new things. That's a trade-off, not a fault.

Here's the move that turns opinions into analysis. Separate a change in the task from a change in its form, meaning how the task gets done. Take friends. A sixteen-year-old in the nineties cared a lot about what friends thought, and so does a sixteen-year-old today. The task hasn't changed. Its form has. Friends were once the people in the room or on the home phone. Now they're available all the time, the group is bigger, and approval arrives as a public number.

scenes.title: identity and autonomy, in a new form

voiceover.text: The same test works on the other tasks. Identity formation hasn't changed, but now there's a searchable, long-lasting public record of earlier versions of you. Autonomy hasn't changed either, but its form has stretched out. Study lasts longer, financial independence comes later, and people leave home later. That longer stretch between adolescence and settled adult life is called emerging adulthood.

The syllabus asks about five influences, and each one has a constant and a change. Family is still the first source of health habits, but households are more varied and young people depend on them for longer. Peers matter as much as ever, now continuously. Culture still sets the norms, but some have shifted, so smoking is far less normal, and talking about mental health is more accepted. Every generation adopts new technology faster than adults, but one device now carries school, friends and advertising. And global events always shape a generation, but news now arrives instantly and never stops.

So how do you make a generational claim that holds up? Use four tests. First, is it the age, or the era? Adults describing young people are often just describing being young. Second, compared with what, and measured how? More diagnoses can mean more people seeking help, not more illness. Third, which young people? The differences within a generation are usually bigger than the differences between generations. And fourth, does anything follow for health?

Why compare generations in a health course at all? Three reasons. What worked before may not work now: a message built for television and school assemblies won't reach someone whose news arrives through a feed. Some risks have shrunk, like smoking, and some are new, like screens cutting into sleep and comparison that never switches off. And it stops the deficit story, because young people treated as a problem are less likely to use the services meant for them.
Two things to remember. Same task, new form. And the differences within a generation are usually bigger than the differences between them.

Two exam questions. First. A grandparent says, "Teenagers today take far more risks than we ever did." Identify whether this claim describes a change in a developmental task, or in the form of the task, and rewrite it as a claim that could be supported with evidence. Pause here to answer.

The task hasn't changed: risk-taking rises in adolescence in every generation. So the claim is really about form. A defensible version names which risks changed: smoking and drink driving have fallen, and online risks are new. You'd support it with trend data by age. The classic mistake is saying phones made teenagers reckless.
Second. Compare the lives of young people today with those of a previous generation, referring to at least three of the influences on young people's lives. Pause here to answer.

Open with the organising idea: the developmental tasks are the same, so compare the form they take. Then take three influences, each with a similarity and a difference. Peers matter in both, but contact is now continuous. Family still shapes health, but dependence lasts longer. Technology is always adopted first by the young. The classic mistake is a paragraph on then, and a paragraph on now.

So, to compare generations, name the task, name the changed form, check the evidence, and say what follows for health. Which leaves a real question. If the tasks are the same but the conditions have changed, what does health actually mean to young people now? Adults can't answer that on their behalf. Next, we'll learn how to find out properly.
